title: Istanbul Convention withdrawal debate: call for a referendum and absence from the vote (2025)
description: On 30 October 2025, after a 13-hour debate, the Saeima voted 56 to 32 with two abstentions to withdraw Latvia from the Council of Europe's Istanbul Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence, the first EU member state to decide so. Speaking from the rostrum as an opposition MP, Kulbergs called on Prime Minister Evika Siliņa to resign and said withdrawal should be put to a popular vote. According to LSM, he first urged MPs from the rostrum to support withdrawal but then did not take part in the vote, saying health problems had made him leave the sitting early. President Edgars Rinkēvičs did not promulgate the law and returned it to the Saeima, whose majority — the United List and the National Alliance having changed position — set a deadline for proposals of 1 November 2026, leaving the question to the next Saeima. As Prime Minister, Kulbergs said in May 2026 that his coalition would not raise divisive issues such as the convention; LSM reports that he and other United List politicians said during and after the 2026 campaign that the question should be decided by a consultative referendum.
key_facts: 30 October 2025: Saeima votes 56–32–2 to leave the Istanbul Convention
Kulbergs calls for a referendum and for Siliņa's resignation; does not vote, citing health reasons (LSM)
President Rinkēvičs returns the law; it is left to the 15th Saeima
May 2026: as PM-designate, Kulbergs says the coalition will not raise divisive issues

title: Social-media remark that Dainis Īvāns 'deserved a spit in the face' (2025)
description: The day after the Saeima's debate on leaving the Istanbul Convention, Kulbergs reacted on social media to a speech by Dainis Īvāns, the former leader of the Popular Front of Latvia, at a rally in Riga's Dome Square against the decision, writing that he was disappointed in Īvāns and that Īvāns 'deserves a spit in the face for this, especially for comparing this event with the Awakening' (LSM). Asked by followers whether he would really be prepared to do it, he answered in the affirmative, and he refused to withdraw the comments. LSM recalled that the post caused considerable public reaction when it reported his nomination as Prime Minister in May 2026. The sources consulted report no formal consequence.
key_facts: Post about the former Popular Front leader's speech at the rally against leaving the Istanbul Convention
Kulbergs confirmed to followers he would be ready to do it and did not withdraw the remark
Recalled by public broadcaster LSM at his nomination in May 2026

title: Claims about the cost of government meetings with NGOs (2026)
description: In July 2026 Kulbergs said on social media, Latvian Television and Latvian Radio that non-governmental organisations on the Memorandum Council billed the State Chancellery about €18,000 'for sitting' at each meeting, and argued that paying NGOs to represent their members created at least an apparent conflict of interest; the remarks led to calls from several parties to cut NGO funding. LSM's fact-checking unit Re:Check found the figure came from dividing the €200,000 a year paid to the Latvian Civic Alliance by the 11 planned sessions — his press adviser confirmed this calculation — whereas the agreement on the State Chancellery website pays for the council's secretariat, working groups, experts, an annual NGO forum and public communication. Re:Check also noted that the Employers' Confederation (LDDK), which Kulbergs cited as an NGO independent of state money and on whose council he had sat, runs a €730,000 European Social Fund project of which €110,000 comes from the state budget. Re:Check described his interpretation as 'questionable at best and misleading or muddled at worst'.
key_facts: Claim: €18,000 per Memorandum Council meeting
Re:Check: the sum is the annual €200,000 budget divided by 11 planned sessions and covers a wider set of tasks
LDDK, cited as a model, receives state co-financing through an ESF project

title: KNAB check of a Kurzeme trip for possible use of administrative resources in campaigning (2026)
period: August 2026 – (no outcome reported as of October 2026)
description: On Friday 7 August 2026, listed in his official schedule as on a regional visit to Kurzeme, Kulbergs travelled with Finance Minister Māris Kučinskis, Justice Minister Edvards Smiltēns and United List candidates; the alliance published photos of them on a combine harvester beside buses bearing candidates' portraits. On 10 August the Corruption Prevention and Combating Bureau (KNAB) told the LETA agency it would carry out a departmental check (resoriskā pārbaude) into whether the activities of United List representatives, including the Prime Minister, complied with the Pre-election Campaign Law and whether administrative resources had been used. LTV's De facto reported, citing a programme prepared by the alliance's office, that the trip billed as an official working visit had in fact been organised by the United List office and by Liepāja Party leader Uldis Sesks, with many stops linked to alliance members or supporters. Kulbergs said he had no time to campaign and did not believe he was using his office for the campaign, adding that on the combine he had posed as the alliance's prime-ministerial candidate. LSM reported on 22 August that the check was continuing; no result had been reported in the sources consulted by 23 October 2026. A KNAB departmental check is an administrative review, not a criminal proceeding.
key_facts: 10 August 2026: KNAB departmental check under the Pre-election Campaign Law
De facto: the 'regional visit' was organised by the United List office and Uldis Sesks
Kulbergs denies using his office for campaigning
22 August: check still ongoing; outcome not reported

title: Refusal to comply with the Prosecutor General's protest over timber-industry discounts (2026)
description: In June 2026 the Prosecutor General's Office lodged a prosecutor's protest asking the Cabinet to annul, from the date they were issued, parts of earlier government protocol decisions — taken before Kulbergs came to office — that cut prices in long-term contracts of the state forest company Latvijas valsts meži for wood-processing firms; the office said the decisions exceeded the Cabinet's competence and contravened the law on preventing the waste of public funds. Accepting the protest would have required the companies to repay the discounts. On 21 July the Kulbergs government, with ministers unanimous, refused: Kulbergs said it was 'physically impossible' to annul decisions already executed, agreed that in his view the protest was not legally well founded, and said the government would ask the Constitutional Court to clarify its powers; Prosecutor General Armīns Meisters had said the dispute could reach that court. A criminal case opened on 23 March 2026 against ten people, including former agriculture minister Armands Krauze (Union of Greens and Farmers), continues; Kulbergs is not a party to it, and those involved are presumed innocent. When his coalition gave the Agriculture Ministry to the Union of Greens and Farmers again, Kulbergs said the coalition agreement would not tolerate conflicts of interest or breaches of the law.
key_facts: Prosecutor's protest against Cabinet protocol decisions on price cuts for wood processors
21 July 2026: government refuses; Kulbergs: 'you cannot annul something that has been executed'
Constitutional Court explanation to be sought
Separate criminal case against ten people including ex-minister Krauze; Kulbergs not a party

title: Reversal on state support for airBaltic and the Chapter 11 restructuring (2026)
description: In spring 2026, in opposition, the United List voted against or did not vote when the Saeima approved a €30 million short-term state loan to the airline sought by the Siliņa government. As Prime Minister, Kulbergs said on 1 July that 'not a single cent' more would be invested until airBaltic showed how it could fly without state injections. In August his government asked the Saeima for a mandate to extend the €30 million loan, capitalise interest on state-held bonds, convert state claims into shares and possibly buy up to €30 million of new bonds alongside private investors; he called it the 'last chance' to save the airline and said his earlier opposition was due to a lack of information on how the money would be used. Coalition partner the Union of Greens and Farmers opposed the bill, which passed 54–21–1 on 20 August. On 14 September airBaltic began restructuring its debts under Chapter 11 in a New York bankruptcy court under a plan the government presented as its own; LSM noted that the airline has no flights to or within the United States. Kulbergs also asked for government decisions on airBaltic over the past 20 years to be declassified. In October the court approved in final form up to €350 million of private debtor-in-possession financing; a hearing on giving those lenders priority over the 2029 bondholders is set for November.
key_facts: United List opposed the spring 2026 €30 million loan
1 July 2026: 'not a single cent' without a viable plan
20 August 2026: stabilisation law adopted 54–21–1, ZZS against
14 September 2026: Chapter 11 filing; 20 October: final court approval of up to €350 million DIP financing

title: U-turn on restricting Russian grain transit (October 2026)
description: After the Saeima urgently amended the Railway Law on 17 September 2026 to allow a rapid increase in rail infrastructure fees for grain shipped from Russia, the government decided to raise those fees by 300%. On 13 October Kulbergs said after a cabinet meeting that neither the increase nor a ban was currently possible: the EU has exclusive competence over tariffs and transit, contracts for 300,000 tonnes had already been signed, and ministers had been told a ban could expose Latvia to legal claims of €200–800 million. He acknowledged that the government had not been fully aware of the facts when it decided the increase. He also argued that the grain 'does not belong to Russia at all' but to large corporations from strategic partners such as the United States, Switzerland and Japan; LSM noted that he did not say whether this reasoning would apply to other sectors. Estonia had meanwhile imposed national sanctions banning Russian and Belarusian grain transit. Kulbergs, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda asked EU leaders for an EU-wide ban.
key_facts: Government decision to raise Russian grain transit fees by 300% not applied
Kulbergs cites EU competence and a €200–800 million litigation risk
Kulbergs: the transiting grain belongs to companies from strategic partner countries
Joint Baltic letter calling for an EU ban

title: Call to drop the streaming-platform ('Netflix') levy, citing relations with the US (October 2026)
description: Right after the 3 October 2026 election, Kulbergs told the LETA agency that the government should consider dropping a planned obligation for streaming platforms to invest at least 3.5% of their Latvian revenue in local film and series production, which a Saeima committee had just sent for accelerated adoption. He said Latvia would not 'put on edge' relations with its strategic partner the United States for about €600,000, and that he had supported the levy earlier because he did not know what the reaction and consequences would be. Three film-industry organisations wrote to him and to the President in protest, and Culture Minister Nauris Puntulis (National Alliance) said he hoped only a postponement was meant. The Saeima then passed the bills in second reading but removed their urgency. On 13 October, after meeting the industry, Kulbergs proposed postponing the decision and giving the film sector an extra €1 million from 2027 without naming a funding source; the industry called this a temporary compromise and said it would keep pressing for the levy.
key_facts: Levy: at least 3.5% of platforms' previous-year Latvian revenue for local content
Kulbergs: relations with the US outweigh about €600,000 a year
Saeima removes urgency; Kulbergs offers €1 million a year more for film from 2027

title: Welfare Minister Reinis Uzulnieks arrested for drunk driving (September 2026)
period: September 2026 – (criminal case pending as of October 2026)
description: On 12 September 2026 police stopped Welfare Minister Reinis Uzulnieks (Union of Greens and Farmers, ZZS), a member of the Kulbergs cabinet, driving with a blood alcohol level reported by LTV at 3.5 per mille; he was held at a temporary detention centre. The next day the ZZS board decided to remove him from the ministry and expel him from the party, and Uldis Augulis was appointed acting Welfare Minister. Kulbergs called the act 'particularly irresponsible and categorically unacceptable' and the dismissal 'the only correct decision'. On 24 September Uzulnieks was charged under Section 262(1.1) of the Criminal Law with driving with a blood alcohol level above 1.5 per mille, punishable by up to one year in prison; he stayed on the ZZS list, which failed to re-enter the Saeima. Kulbergs is not a party to the case, and Uzulnieks is presumed innocent until a court rules.
key_facts: 12 September 2026: minister caught driving drunk; removed by his party the next day
Kulbergs backs the dismissal
24 September 2026: charged under Section 262(1.1) of the Criminal Law
Kulbergs is not a party to the proceedings

title: Public rebuke of Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava over the migration plan (September 2026)
description: On 1 September 2026 Kulbergs publicly criticised the report on implementing a parliamentary inquiry's migration recommendations that Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava (National Alliance) had submitted an hour and a half before a coalition meeting. He said the minister had been given the task at the beginning of June, had not completed coordination with the institutions concerned and should deliver 'a concrete, actionable offer ... not a story about what prevented him from preparing it'. The document contained more than 70 measures; the State Chancellery, several ministries and employers' organisations objected to parts of it, the Economics Ministry for example to a separate working-time accounting system for third-country nationals. Kulbergs said he fully supported a stricter migration policy but that migration was too serious to be part of 'the pre-election competition for the loudest slogans'. The coalition agreed on further steps to bring a document to the cabinet; the outcome was not reported in the sources consulted.
key_facts: Report with more than 70 measures submitted on 31 August 2026
Kulbergs publicly faults its preparation and coordination
Objections from ministries and employers' organisations
